10.1149/ma2025-02251397mtgabs.abstract: The electrochemical synthesis of ammonia (NH 3 ) presents a promising avenue for sustainable industrial production, particularly via lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reactions (NRR). This study explores innovations in reactor architecture and electrode materials while focusing on process efficiency for NH 3 electrosynthesis. A major challenge in NRR lies in overcoming the strong nitrogen triple bond and suppressing the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), which lowers the Faradaic efficiency (FE) of NH 3 production [1],[2] . The conventional Haber-Bosch process, while effective, operates at extreme conditions of temperature and pressure, consuming vast amounts of energy and emitting significant CO 2 . Electrochemical NH 3 synthesis, by contrast, offers a pathway to decentralized and sustainable production, particularly if renewable electricity is employed. However, the sluggish kinetics of N 2 activation combined with parasitic HER, necessitate careful optimization of electrode materials and reaction conditions. Initial experiments using a nickel as working (WE), platinum as counter (CE) and silver as reference (RE) electrodes in an electrochemical cell with a lithium-based catalyst, as previously reported in literature [3] , demonstrated low NH 3 yield and high current instability. A recurring issue were the fluctuations in the applied potential and the inconsistent lithium plating behavior, due to the lack of a reliable RE in terms of potential drifts. Through iterative reactor design optimizations—including modifications in working electrode (WE) surface area and the integration of a bubbler – an improvement of the initial yield of 0.08% Faradaic efficiency (FE) at -3.2 V Li plating potential to 6.75% FE at -3.1V was achieved. Further, the long-term stability was improved, enabling the system to be operated up to at least 6 hours. Despite these improvements, potential stability and RE reliability limitations remained. Thus, the importance of FE deriving from dependable current recording was highlighted as a reactor evaluation metric, along with the significance of the RE as a reliable indicator of electrode performance and stability in the electrochemical cell. Therefore, the investigation on finding a stable RE followed next. To address RE limitations, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) [4] was tested as alternative to the Ag/Ag⁺ pseudoreference electrode. The LFP-based RE exhibited lower noise and better reproducibility in lithium-containing organic electrolytes, improving potential control during lithium plating and nitrogen reduction. Further, potentio-profile importation (PPI) used in another study [5] was explored alongside constant voltage (CstV) application. CstV, utilized pulsed potentiostatic intervals with open-circuit rests instead of 0 V application, an approach that provided minimized side reactions and charge accumulations as seen on the potential evolution of the counter electrode and the current evolution over time (Figure A,B), potentially leading to more targeted NH₃ production. Having the new reactor design as a starting point and the current and potential instabilities observed on the initial studies, a method based on calibration experiments utilizing ferrocene (Fc) was proposed to establish an optimized potential range for lithium plating and reliable electrochemical measurements. Specifically, the initial cyclic voltammetry step is confined to a short window range aiming to evaluate the state of the RE without starting lithium plating as proposed in literature [3] in order for the CstV to target the NRR and define the reaction FE for comparative studies. Taking a closer look on the current-time traces, it could be noticed that the experiment did not follow a typical Cottrell’s equation curve [6] when slight applied potential shifts were made (Figure C, D). Based on that observation, efforts to mitigate excessive lithium deposition and HER side reactions were explored through tailored current density modulation and pulse plating techniques. Further advancements in electrochemical cell engineering, electrocatalyst development and reaction monitoring techniques will be crucial in driving the transition toward sustainable nitrogen fixation technologies. The insights gained from this study contribute to the better understanding of the electrocatalytic mechanism nitrogen and lithium follow to produce ammonia, using a batch electrochemical cell, paving the way to improvements on the selectivity of the reaction and its optimized efficiency. The studied reactor design is being optimized for reliable current measurements to properly evaluate reaction efficiencies, and it is suitable for adaptation to continuous-flow experiments. Additionally, this work underscores the importance of fundamental electrochemical principles in optimizing reaction conditions while considering a long-term operating, continuous-flow reactor design, towards the transition of laboratory knowledge to industrial practices. 10.1149/ma2025-02281539mtgabs.abstract: Green ammonia production via electrolysis using renewable and low-cost electrons is a promising pathway to compete with the traditional Haber-Bosch process. According to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) and National Renewable Energy Lab (NREL), the projected average levelized cost of energy (LCOE) could reach 0.03 $/kWh by 2030, a promising lower price point than fossil fuel-driven electricity generation. The nitrogen-containing compounds required for ammonia production can be sourced from various sources, including wastewater and exhaust gas, reinforcing the nitrogen circular economy. Various cell configurations, flow cells, and batch cells affect the electrochemical cell performance and efficiency. In addition to the choice of cell design, selecting the right proton donor, such as hydrogen, water, and water vapor, is crucial to achieve the highest cell energy efficiency. The economic feasibility of ammonia production strongly depends on electrolyzer size. Evaluating proper dimensions for the electrolyzer, considering its operation schedule and production stream, necessitates optimization based on the dynamic or static operation of the plant. In this presentation, We look at multiple electrochemical pathways for ammonia production using various nitrogen feedstocks, including from wastewater via nitrate (NO 3 - ) and nitrite (NO 2 - ) reduction, from exhaust gas via nitric oxide (NO), nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ), and nitrous oxide (N 2 O) reduction, and finally from the air via nitrogen gas (N 2 ) reduction. We optimize the levelized cost of ammonia (LCOA) by choosing anodic and cathodic feedstocks, cell configurations, temperature, and dynamic or static operation. We model and compare cell voltage, faradaic and energy efficiencies considering activation overpotential, Nernstian, and ohmic losses. Finally, we identify the most optimized pathway for green ammonia production from each feedstock.

10.1149/ma2025-02281543mtgabs.abstract: Ammonia is a necessary fertilizer and chemical in industrial processes. However, the conventional Haber-Bosch process for ammonia synthesis consumes 1% of the world’s total energy production and accounts for 1.4% of global carbon dioxide emissions. Electrochemical Li-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) presents a favorable alternative because it allows for ammonia synthesis with a lower CO 2 footprint at mild conditions. Given the expensive cost of Li sources, recovering Li from abundant brine, and improving Li utilization in ammonia synthesis would improve its sustainability and efficiency. Herein, we have developed a new electrochemical strategy to achieve ammonia production and Li + recovery from brine using a Li-ion selective redox material. We choose λ-MnO 2 as the redox material and synthesize it by delithiating nanosized lithium manganese oxide. The λ-MnO 2 electrode can selectively extract Li + and exhibits excellent electrochemical stability in brine with a high ratio of Na + / Li + over 50 cycles. We propose to use recovered Li + and subsequently deposited Li method as a mediator to electrochemically reduce N 2 to NH 3 as fertilizer and produce high-purity Li salts simultaneously. This work introduces a new strategy for simultaneous sustainable ammonia production and Li recovery from brine, contributing to advancements in environmentally friendly integrated electrosynthesis and resource recovery.

10.1149/ma2025-02291550mtgabs.abstract: Ammonia is a critical industrial chemical and potential carbon-neutral energy carrier, yet its conventional ammonia production via the Haber-Bosch process requires harsh conditions (400-500°C, up to 200 bar) and generates significant carbon emissions. The lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) has emerged as a promising alternative for sustainable ammonia synthesis at ambient conditions. However, Li-NRR efficiency is limited by electrolyte design challenges, as traditional electrolytes either suffer from poor selectivity (low-concentration electrolytes, LCE) or face issues with high viscosity and cost (high-concentration electrolytes, HCE). To improve the efficiency of Li-NRR, we first introduce a localized high-concentration electrolyte (LHCE) that enables the formation of anion-derived SEI. This study employs experimental and computational approaches to elucidate the superior performance of electrolytes in Li-NRR for ammonia synthesis. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we comprehensively analyzed the solvation structures in LCE, HCE, and LHCE systems. Our computational results reveal that LHCE exhibits the highest anion-to-solvent ratio in the lithium coordination sphere among all electrolyte configurations, despite having the same salt concentration as LCE. The simulations demonstrate that the antisolvent in LHCE effectively modifies the local environment around lithium ions, promoting anion-rich solvation structures. Experimentally, we observed that this computationally confirmed higher anion ratio in LHCE directly corresponds to superior Faradaic efficiency in ammonia production compared to both LCE and HCE systems. Spectroscopic analyses validate the predicted solvation structures, confirming the computational model's accuracy. This work establishes a fundamental connection between anion-rich solvation structures and enhanced Li-NRR performance, providing a computational framework for rational electrolyte design in electrochemical ammonia synthesis. 10.1149/ma2025-02303534mtgabs.abstract: Electrochemical nitrate reduction offers a sustainable, electricity-driven route to convert nitrate into ammonia, simultaneously removing a pollutant and producing a valuable product for a circular nitrogen economy. However, most catalysts face challenges with selectivity, high cost, and low stability. We present a hierarchical three-dimensional electrode that combines a porous copper foam scaffold, a conductive graphene interlayer, and a metal-organic framework (MOF) coating to enable efficient and selective nitrate-to-ammonia conversion under ambient conditions. The copper foam provides high surface area and conductivity, graphene lowers charge-transfer resistance and enhances durability, and MOF metal sites accelerate multi-electron transfer toward ammonia. Electrochemical studies show that the integrated Cu/Gr/MOF electrode achieves higher current densities, lower onset potential, and a threefold increase in ammonia yield compared to bare or graphene-coated copper. Composed of low-cost, earth-abundant materials, this scalable architecture highlights a promising direction for practical nitrate-to-ammonia electrocatalysis.

10.1149/ma2025-02311602mtgabs.abstract: The continued downscaling of electronic device dimensions requires the development of new, precise patterning methods that are compatible with high-volume manufacturing. Area selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD) continues to gain attention as an important method to achieve nanoscale features at the sub-10 nm length scale. It is known that tuning the surface chemistry of the substrate can be used to either inhibit or enhance ALD nucleation, leading to selective deposition. Since the initial introduction of AS-ALD 20 years ago, a key strategy has been the use of inhibitors, ranging from long-chain self-assembled monolayers to small molecule inhibitors, which can alter the native surface reactivity to block nucleation. This inhibition approach enables good selectivity in AS-ALD of thin films on a variety of substrate materials, including dielectrics and metals, and is in use today. I will present several inhibitor-based AS-ALD systems. As the field moves forward, however, additional process parameters will need to be tuned if we are to meet future AS-ALD application requirements, which are now dictating a wide breadth of materials systems (including dielectric/dielectric, metal/dielectric, carbon/dielectric, multicolor patterns, etc.) as well as a high degree of selectivity. I will introduce some of the approaches under development, including tuning the ALD precursor in concert with the inhibitor. Results show that precursor size can have a significant influence on the ability of inhibitors to prevent ALD nucleation; for example, larger precursors can provide for selectivity even when less inhibitory blocking molecules are used. However, precursor size alone is not the defining metric, and I will share examples that highlight the influence of other precursor effects, such as precursor-inhibitor reactivity and miscibility. Ultimately, developing molecular design rules for both inhibitors and ALD precursors will be critical for applying AS-ALD more widely to future challenges in microelectronics fabrication.

10.1149/ma2025-02311605mtgabs.abstract: Introduction Large-Scale Integrations (LSIs) have been improved performance through the development of scaling technology, and further technological development is required for miniaturization in the future. Cu is currently used as the interconnect layer of LSIs. In general, an additional barrier layer such as titanium nitride or tantalum nitride is required to avoid the Cu diffusion, and then, the interconnect resistance gradually increases as miniaturization of LSIs proceeds [1] because of the high resistivity of barrier material. From the above, Ru is attractive interconnect material since it has low resistance at nanoscale region and does not need the barrier metals in different to Cu [1]. Furthermore, the number of lithography steps can be reduced by applying ASALD (Area Selective Atomic Layer Deposition), leading to cost saving [2]. This is a promising approach for bottom-up patterning and holds the potential to be an addition to traditional patterning methods [2]. In this study, we performed ASALD of Ru by using inhibitor with W as the growth surface and SiO₂ as the non-growth surface. Experiments The inhibitor was applied to W and SiO 2 surfaces fabricated by sputtering and the chemical vapor deposition (CVD), respectively, on Si wafers, and Ru was deposited by ALD on the both surfaces after inhibitor treated and the cleaning. The ALD cycles were set from 100 to 500 cycles. The Ru thickness was measured using X-ray fluorescence. We also prepared patterned samples to investigate the selective growth on the line and space (L&S) pattern with W and SiO 2 . Figure 1 shows process flow of patterned wafers. W (50 nm) was deposited on the Si substrate by sputtering, Si 3 N 4 (10 nm) and SiO 2 (30 nm) by the CVD. Then, SiO 2 and Si 3 N 4 were etched by the reactive ion etching (RIE) using CF 4 and H 2 . The L&S was set to1:1 with a pattern width of 2 μm. Then, the inhibitor was treated to all surface to form the non-growth areas, and clean for W surfaces. Finally, Ru was deposited by ALD using [Ru(TMM)(CO) 3 ] (TMM = trimethylenemethane) with oxygen as the reactant. The oxygen exposure time was 2 sec/cycle. ALD performed at relatively low deposition temperature of 250 ℃ along with a high growth per cycle of 0.16 nm. Evaluation of area selective deposition was performed by the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observation and the energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) measurements. Results and discussion Figure 2 shows the ALD cycle dependence of Ru film thickness on each blanket W and SiO 2 surfaces with or without the inhibitor treatment. Regardless of the inhibitor treatment, Ru can be deposited on W. In contrast, Ru cannot be deposited on SiO 2 with inhibitor treatment. This means the inhibitor works only on SiO 2 surface after the treatment of inhibitor adsorption. We consider that chemical adsorption of the inhibitor on SiO 2 surface, resulting in the presence of the inhibitor even after the treatment. Although the inhibitors on SiO 2 were exposed to oxygen for a total of 1000 sec (2 sec × 500) the inhibitor continues to work with high Ru deposition inhibition on SiO 2 . Figure 3 shows the SEM-EDX mapping on patterned wafers with the inhibitor. We found that selective growth of Ru occurs exclusively on W in the patterned wafers. Traditionally, high selectivity could be achieved through the integration of ALD and Atomic Layer Etching (ALE) [3]. In contrast, the selective deposition can be performed by only ALD with the inhibitor. Conclusion The inhibitor treatment can promote the area selective deposition of Ru on W without deposition on SiO 2 by only ALD. This method is the one of the most effective candidate for the interconnect formation method in future LSI. 10.1149/ma2025-02311606mtgabs.abstract: Area-selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD) is a promising technique for advanced nanofabrication processes. This allows for the simple bottom-up creation of intricate nanostructures essential for advanced optoelectronic and sensor applications. 1 Due to the flexibility of ALD, the method can be used alongside its organic counterpart, molecular layer deposition (MLD). 2 The combined atomic/molecular layer deposition (ALD/MLD) enables tuning of material properties by incorporating organic linkers into the film while maintaining the nanoscale control. 3 Area-selective ALD and MLD separately have been demonstrated previously, but these processes typically rely on utilization of inhibitors and lithography steps to achieve the area-selectivity, which complicates the process. 4,5 While there are examples of AS-ALD being used on two-dimensional materials (2DM), AS-MLD on them is still mostly unexplored. Due to the inherent 2D nature, the surface of 2DM does not provide sufficient reactive sites for the chemisorption of ALD/MLD precursors compared with traditional microelectronics. Surface functionalization can provide the selective 3D growth of desired materials. Recently, we have overcome the chemical inertness of graphene to ALD precursors by local activation using direct femtosecond laser two-photon oxidation (TPO) 6 for selective ZnO deposition. 7 In this study, we guided the growth of Europium-terephthalate thin films on top of single-layer graphene via TPO. 8 We achieved high homogeneity and more than 90% selectivity in locally activated predefined regions for thicknesses up to 11 nm. The deposited thin films exhibited intriguing photoluminescent properties, broadening the material's characteristic excitation wavelength from ultraviolet to the visible light range. The work function, Raman spectroscopy, and fluorescence lifetime imaging data confirmed electronic interactions and n-type doping of TPO graphene after ALD/MLD. The demonstrated approach provides a path forward for integrating 2DM-based heterostructures into optoelectronic, photonic, and energy-harvesting devices. Sub-micron precision achieved in this work expands the design possibilities for multifunctional devices on a single chip. References Parsons G. N., Clark R. 10.1149/ma2025-02311632mtgabs.abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal disulfides (2D-TMDs) have attracted significant research interest as potential replacements for noble metal electrocatalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction [1]. Among these materials, the metallic compound NbS 2 has more recently emerged as a promising candidate due to its high conductivity and catalytically active basal plane sites, which contribute to low overpotentials and high efficiency [2]. Several methods have been used to prepare NbS 2 electrodes, including coating exfoliated nanoflakes on support materials, solvothermal synthesis and chemical vapor deposition, but these approaches have significant drawbacks relating to scalability, consistency, and device integration [1]. In contrast, atomic layer deposition (ALD) can produce films with good adhesion, tunable materials properties, and conformal coating of porous and architectured substrates, making it a promising technique to produce catalyst materials for electrolyzers [3]. In this work, we demonstrate atomic layer deposition of thin films containing NbS 2 using an organometallic Nb precursor (tert-butylimido tris-diethylamino niobium(V)) and an H 2 S/H 2 plasma coreactant step. Control of film composition and microstructure is enabled by tuning of ALD process parameters and post-deposition annealing treatments. In particular, the H 2 S/H 2 ratio used during the plasma step provides control of the niobium/sulfur ratio of the film, which is desirable because favorable catalytic performance has been reported for materials with Nb/S ratios different from 1/2 [4]. Also, the crystallinity and morphology of the film depend on ALD deposition temperature and H 2 S/H 2 plasma ratio and can be further modulated by annealing. The tunable materials properties of ALD-grown films are then correlated with catalytic performance through electrochemical testing in acidic solution. 10.1149/ma2025-02311634mtgabs.abstract: The economic ramifications associated with the utilization of noble metals/precious metals such as Pt, Pd, Ir, Rh, and Ru are significant, as they are not only costly but also relatively scarce, with Ir being especially limited, given that its natural occurrence is estimated to be roughly one-tenth that of Pt and Ru, rendering its availability a crucial element in industrial electrocatalysis and sensing applications. In this regard, atomic layer deposition (ALD) emerges as a cutting-edge precision thin film technique that is increasingly recommended for industrial applications, as it provides atomic-level control over the deposition of even the rarest noble metals Ir, allowing for the placement of single metal atoms or clusters through a self-limiting growth process. We attempt to introduce a pragmatic approach towards the utilization of Ir precious metal, employing the ALD technique on the ever-expanding new 2D MXene family member, thereby facilitating the creation of a sophisticated Ir-ALD-MXene advanced multifunctional heterostructure that not only takes into account the cost and rarity of Ir but also aims to contribute significantly to next-generation hydrogen fuel and human-machine interfaced healthcare applications. We observe a steady improvement of over 250% in electrocatalytic activities and 400 % in outstanding sensitivity of Ir-ALD-MXene by smartly controlling the Ir-ALD cycle numbers compared to the pristine MXene. Noteworthy is the observation that the presence of Ir in the form of single atoms or clusters significantly enhances the surface catalytic and sensing activity; thus, given its limited earth abundancy, the improved catalytic-sensing performance per iridium atom, achieved with a considerably reduced quantity of the precious metals, has been comprehensively examined through computational techniques as well as next-generation aberration-corrected ultra-high-resolution electron microscopies. The current research contributes substantially to the field by establishing precise and delicate control over the arrangement of the precious metals through an emerging ALD process technique for creating new ALD precious metal-based electrocatalysts and healthcare sensors on ever-expanding MXene 2D nanomaterials. 10.1149/ma2025-02311635mtgabs.abstract: The widespread application of hydrogen fuel cells relies heavily on high performance oxygen reduction reaction catalysts. When facing with complex and harsh operational conditions, traditional Pt-based catalysts always surfer from serious electrochemical corrosion or poisoning of sulfonic acid groups at the catalyst or cell level. Previous approaches developed to mitigate unsaturated site dissolution in Pt-based hydrogen fuel cell electrocatalysts often lead to dealloying and reduced electrochemically active areas. In this talk, a series of highly stable Pt-based alloy catalysts are prepared by ultrathin metal oxide coating and post-annealing process, which could avoid the agglomeration of catalyst particles caused by high ordering temperature. A sub-surface interstitial doping strategy is proposed to effectively modulate local lattice strain and the electronic structures of unstable surface sites on Pt based nanoparticles using atomic layer deposition. Notably, the sub-surface interstitial doping of boron atoms significantly enhances the dissolution resistance of the Pt and Pt alloy nanoparticles. In situ experiments combined with theoretical calculations reveal that the boron-induced asymmetric tensile strain on the surface effectively weakens the adsorption of key oxygen species by the unsaturated nanoparticle sites. Furthermore, continuous electron donation from boron to platinum inhibits oxidative corrosion, thereby boosting the electrocatalytic durability. At the cell level, spatially confined ultrafine Pt-based alloy in porous carbon support could effectively improve the performance of fuel cells by reducing oxygen transport resistance. References 1. 10.1149/ma2025-02311646mtgabs.abstract: Next-generation lithium-ion batteries demand cathode materials that not only deliver high energy density but also maintain electrochemical reversibility over prolonged cycling. Among the various cathode candidates, single-crystalline lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (SC-NMC) has emerged as a promising material due to its superior structural integrity and resistance to grain boundary-related degradation compared to polycrystalline NMC (PC-NMC). However, despite the enhanced bulk stability of SC-NMC, it remains susceptible to surface degradation, particularly under high-voltage conditions. These surface-related issues primarily stem from parasitic side reactions between the active material and the liquid electrolyte, resulting in the formation of an unstable and resistive cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI) layer. This non-uniform CEI hinders lithium-ion transport, induces localized volume changes, and promotes the formation of internal microcracks during repeated cycling. Ultimately, such degradation mechanisms severely compromise the electrochemical performance and long-term stability of SC-NMC cathodes, limiting their practical application in high-energy-density battery systems. To overcome these challenges, we employed a surface engineering strategy utilizing powder-based atomic layer deposition (Powder-ALD) to form a conformal, nanometer-scale protective layer on the SC-NMC surface. Specifically, molybdenum oxide (MoOₓ) was selected as the coating material due to its favorable properties, including high electronic and lithium-ion conductivity, as well as excellent electrochemical and chemical stability. The Powder-ALD process was conducted using a custom-built rotary-type ALD reactor designed for powder samples, enabling uniform coating coverage on all surfaces of the SC-NMC particles. The coating thickness was systematically varied from 1 to 5 nm (corresponding to 10 to 50 ALD cycles) to investigate the impact of layer thickness on electrochemical performance and to identify the optimal coating conditions. The MoOₓ layer functions as an artificial CEI that effectively passivates the reactive surface of the cathode while preserving fast lithium-ion kinetics. Owing to its conformal nature, the ALD-derived coating accommodates mechanical strain and minimizes structural deterioration during charge–discharge cycling. Electrochemical evaluations conducted under various operating conditions demonstrated the effectiveness of the MoOₓ coating. Under a cut-off voltage of 4.3 V and a 1C rate for 100 cycles, the MoOₓ-coated SC-NMC electrode showed an approximately 5% increase in initial discharge capacity compared to the uncoated sample, while achieving 97% capacity retention. Furthermore, under a more aggressive condition of 4.5 V cut-off voltage at a 2C rate for 100 cycles, the coated cathodes retained about 90% of their capacity, highlighting their robustness under high-voltage, high-rate cycling. To further validate the effectiveness of MoOₓ as a cathode coating material, a comparative study was conducted with SC-NMC particles coated with zirconium oxide (ZrO₂), a material known for its surface passivation and moderate lithium-ion conductivity. Although ZrO₂ effectively suppresses electrolyte decomposition, the MoOₓ-coated samples outperformed ZrO₂-coated ones in both capacity retention and rate capability, suggesting that MoOₓ offers superior interfacial conductivity and structural stabilization. Our findings underscore the critical role of nanoscale surface modification in enhancing the electrochemical durability of SC-NMC cathodes. The Powder-ALD approach ensures precise thickness control and uniform deposition, even on complex three-dimensional morphologies typical of battery powder materials. Moreover, the application of a conductive and electrochemically stable oxide such as MoOₓ introduces additional advantages, including improved charge transport and prolonged cycling stability under harsh operating conditions. This study demonstrates that MoOₓ-based ALD coatings represent an effective strategy for mitigating surface-driven degradation in high-voltage lithium-ion batteries and provide a viable path toward the commercial viability of SC-NMC materials. Future work will extend this surface modification strategy to solid-state battery systems, enabling comparative electrochemical analysis across multiple battery platforms to further define the essential properties required for advanced cathode coatings.

10.1149/ma2025-02311656mtgabs.abstract: The control of crystal phase, composition, and morphology in multicomponent nanomaterials is a powerful strategy for introducing new, unique physicochemical properties, functionalities, and applications. This contribution details our recent advancements in the rapid non-equilibrium synthesis of functional high-entropy alloy nanocatalysts with enhanced performances in water electrolysis. Precursor noble metal thin layers were deposited sequentially by ALD. Joule heating was then applied in second-range timeframes, promoting atomic diffusion across the individual layers and supercooling kinetics to form homogeneous noble metal high-entropy alloy films. Optimizing precursor film thickness allows control over supercooling kinetics and induces explosive crystallization, forming a multiphasic sub-surface comprising nanocrystalline and amorphous domains through steeper thermal gradients, rapid latent heat release, and quenching dynamics. The resulting noble metal high-entropy alloy thin films demonstrated attractive HER performance with low overpotentials, ranging from 13 to 65 mV at a current density of 10 mA cm −2 , and low Tafel slopes from 14 to 78 mV dec −1 , indicating fast kinetics across acidic, neutral, and alkaline electrolyte conditions. We further demonstrated the formation of amorphous metal phosphate films that showcased outstanding OER overpotentials as low as 235 mV and Tafel slopes between 30 to 40 mV dec −1 , as well as maintaining long-term stability up to 100 hours at a constant current of 10 mA cm −2 in an alkaline aqueous medium. Detailed structural analyses using cyclic voltammetry, high-resolution electron microscopy, X-ray-based energy-dispersive spectroscopy and photoelectron spectroscopy, as well as Raman spectroscopy, elucidate how the intrinsic amorphous structure of these materials facilitates rapid charge transfer and surface reconstruction, thereby enhancing HER/OER performance.

10.1149/ma2025-02381817mtgabs.abstract: Storing energy in the nitrogen cycle (N 2 ⇌ N-based fuel) is a promising and thorny route towards energy sustainability. Hydrazine (N 2 H 4 ) is a key nitrogen compound, ubiquitous in nature and in chemical applications. Since the 1940s, anhydrous hydrazine has been used as a rocket fuel, good for its energetic oxidation by O 2 . The hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR, N 2 H 4 + 4OH – → N 2 + 4H 2 O + 4 e – ) is especially promising as an electrode reaction in direct liquid fuel cells and for hydrazine-assisted hydrogen evolution. Electrocatalysis of the HzOR is both a practical goal, and a scientific paradox: although hydrazine is a famous reductant in chemical synthesis, the overpotential for hydrazine electro-oxidation reaction is still highly dependent on the catalytic surface. Some excellent catalysts have been developed in recent years towards this goal, designed for direct hydrazine fuel cells, electrolyzers, and sensors. Most of these catalysts, however, are either prohibitively expensive (e.g. Pt-based ones), or easily deactivated and NH 3 -producing (e.g Co- and Ni-based materials). Thus, despite the fact that hydrazine has the highest theoretical fuel cell voltage vs. oxygen (1.56 V), and despite decades of research, no practical solutions have been proposed yet. We now report that engineering the first and second coordination spheres of the Fe-N 4 center in a Fe-N-C material opens up a new approach to hydrazine oxidation. A nanometric catalytic pocket was designed in a biomimetic fashion, taking inspiration from the non-planarity (or “ruffleness”) of the Fe-N 4 hemes in hydrazine dehydrogenase, an enzyme for hydrazine oxidation. Creating a “ruffled” FeN 2+2 C 4+4 site lead to a higher accessibility of reactants to the active site, and better bubble removal. This led in turn to a dramatic improvement in activity both in RDE testing and in full MEA testing in an AEM fuel cell, with record-breaking OCV for an Fe-based site. This site could further be installed efficiently on model supports (SLG) but also on cost-effective biowaste supports, re-opening the discussion on using this energy-dense fuel.

10.1149/ma2025-02401945mtgabs.abstract: Since the first Anion-Exchange Membrane (AEM) Fuel Cell (AEMFC) with practical performance was announced about a decade ago 1 , significant advances have been achieved in this field of research. In the past few years of intensive research on AEMFCs, remarkable progress has been reported, such as new highly stable functional groups for advanced AEMs 2-5 and highly active PGM-free catalysts 6-8 . At the cell level, new AEMFCs based on CRM-free catalysts were successfully demonstrated 9 , AEMFC’s lifetime of 5,000-15,000 hours was theoretically demonstrated for the first time 10-11 , and a cell lifetime of 2,000 hours was experimentally proven 12 . Altogether, the research community has made very impressive progress in such a short time. However, many challenges still need to be overcome to achieve AEMFCs of industrial interest. Among them, AEM degradation and AEMFC performance stability are of serious concern. We, at Technion, have recently presented the first results of AEMs and AEMFCs that can be operated at cell temperatures above 100 ℃ 13-17 . At these high temperatures, we could achieve not only high hydroxide ion conductivities close to 300 mS/cm 18 (!) but also improved cell stability (yes, a very counterintuitive result). In turn, these high temperatures allow us to increase the catalyst activity towards both HOR and ORR, allowing the design of first high-performance high-temperature AEMFCs (HT-AEMFCs) made of PGM-free catalysts in both electrodes, and their operation with ambient air. This represents a significant landmark for this technology. In this talk, I will present the achievements and the new state-of-the-art of these HT-AEMFCs. 10.1149/ma2025-02472321mtgabs.abstract: Exploring efficient and durable electrocatalysts under industrial-level current densities is highly desirable for nitrate reduction to ammonia; however, it remains a significant challenge. Herein, we propose Ce-substituted Co 3 O 4 supported on nitrogen-doped carbon that achieves a remarkable NH 3 production rate of 230 mg h -1 mg cat -1 with a FE of 95%, as well as long-term stability of 30 h at a high current density of 1.0 A cm -2 ,superior to previously reported values. In situ spectroscopic and theoretical calculation results reveal that the high electronegativity of Ce triggers the electron redistribution in Co 3 O 4 through the Ce-O-Co network, which boosts surface reconstruction. Such rapid reconstruction leads to the formation of a thin amorphous Co(OH) 2 layer, optimizing the generation of H * towards superior ammonia yields. Moreover, the Ce-O unit plays a protective role under high currents, confining reconstruction to the surface. This study provides an effective strategy for controlling the surface reconstruction of spinel catalysts during NO 3 RR.

10.1149/ma2025-02472323mtgabs.abstract: Nitrate-contaminated water poses a health risk to humans and negatively impacts the ecosystem through eutrophication. While traditional nitrate-removal methods seek to convert the reactive nitrogen species to inert dinitrogen, we propose to valorize nitrate by electrochemically reducing it to ammonia. Ammonia can be used as a fertilizer, chemical precursor, or alternative fuel. Electrochemical methods of water treatment can be implemented in both urban and rural settings because they are modular and can be operated at small through large scales, can be run at ambient temperature and pressure, and can use any source of electricity for power. Here we investigate the impact of ions typically found in groundwater (e.g., calcium, chloride, etc.) on the electrochemical reduction of nitrate to ammonia. In situ attenuated total reflectance–surface-enhanced infrared adsorption spectroscopy (ATR–SEIRAS) is used to probe the impact of water contaminants on adsorbed reactants and reaction intermediates. In situ surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) is employed to reveal the surface-deactivation mechanisms of these contaminants. The in situ spectroscopy results are correlated with product analysis experiments to measure the selectivity and efficiency of ammonia synthesis. Gaseous products are measured by gas chromatography (GC) and liquid products are quantified by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). The goal of our study is to identify strategies to prevent cathode deactivation, such as operating conditions and catalyst surface modification, that enable electrochemical nitrate reduction to ammonia in typical groundwater compositions without additional purification or chemical additives.

10.1149/ma2025-02472324mtgabs.abstract: Ammonia, historically essential as a fertilizer, is now emerging as a carbon-free energy carrier due to its high hydrogen content and sustainable energy potential. 1 However, current NH₃ production relies heavily on the energy-intensive and fossil fuel-dependent Haber-Bosch process. Thus, to meet future NH 3 demand sustainably, the development of innovative green synthesis techniques is essential. 2 On the other hand, nitrates (NO 3 - ), due to their high solubility, represent one of the most widespread pollutants in groundwaters. 3 Increasing NO 3 - concentration in water sources constitutes significant environmental concerns and a serious risk to human health, highlighting the urgent need for the development of novel and efficient removal techniques. 4 In this context, the electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction (E-NO 3 RR) has gained significant attention as it allows the use of renewable electricity for nitrate removal, offering an environmentally friendly approach to water treatment. Moreover, molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2 ), inspired by the roles of molybdenum and sulfur in nitrogenase-based nitrogen fixation, is anticipated to exhibit catalytic activity for E-NO 3 RR. Interestingly, MoS 2 has already demonstrated excellent performance in the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), which competes with E-NO 3 RR under similar conditions, highlighting its potential as a versatile electrocatalyst. 5 In this work, following a prior chemometric optimization, 6 the influence of various elements commonly present in real waters on the E-NO 3 RR performance of a MoS 2 catalyst was systematically evaluated. The experiments were conducted using a flow cell equipped with a gas diffusion electrode, where the catalyst was immobilized via an air-brushing technique. After analyzing the individual effects of different compounds typically found in real waters, a simulated brackish water reverse osmosis brine was employed as the electrolyte in the E-NO 3 RR process. The results revealed significantly lower efficiency when brackish water was used, underscoring the challenges posed by complex water matrices in achieving effective nitrate reduction. 10.1149/ma2025-02472329mtgabs.abstract: Ammonia (NH₃) is the second highest-produced chemical by mass after sulfuric acid.¹,² It is widely used in fertilizers, refrigerants, explosives, textiles, and pharmaceuticals, with growing importance as a green energy carrier and fuel. Commercial ammonia production relies on the thermocatalytic Haber-Bosch process, developed in the early 20th century, which accounts for 1.8% of global energy consumption and emits 0.5 gigatons of CO₂ annually, accounting for 1% of global CO₂ emissions and 15-20% of the chemical sector. Moreover, the rise of processed food and fertilizer industries has disrupted the global nitrogen cycle, causing nitrate accumulation in groundwater and water bodies leading to eutrophication, oxygen depletion, and dead zones.³,⁴ Ammonia electrosynthesis from nitrites under ambient conditions offers a sustainable alternative to simultaneously reduce CO₂ emissions and address nitrate contamination in water bodies. Copper-based catalysts are highly efficient for nitrate reduction reactions (NO₃RR) as cathode electrocatalysts.⁵ However, their slower kinetic and high overpotential requirement of nitrate reduction tends to accumulate nitrite during NO₃RR, leading to a low Faradaic efficiency (FE) for ammonia production.⁶ A series of alloy and spinel oxide electrocatalysts have been synthesized for NO₃RR with a general tradeoff between partial current density and FE which breaks the adsorption-energy scaling relation of copper leading to higher Faradaic efficiency for ammonia production.⁷,⁸ However, there is little to no emphasis on the understanding of electrode kinetics and the role of the spinel structure in NO₃RR remains obfuscated. Most reported metal and spinel oxides excel in alkaline media but face severe facility corrosion; therefore, it is crucial to evaluate NO₃RR in neutral media, considering the presence of nitrate in aquatic environments with a neutral pH. Therefore, this work presents the electrocatalytic nitrate reduction on CuFe₂O₄ in neutral media showing a better yield rate and FE of ammonia formation (98.6% at -0.9 V vs. RHE) compared to that of Cu₂O (78.7% at -0.9 V vs. RHE) with 60% lower accumulation of nitrite in the spent electrolyte after electrolysis, Figure 1 a and b. DFT calculations indicate that the enhanced performance of CuFe₂O₄ compared to Cu₂O arises from several synergistic factors. These include a more favorable surface structure, enabling optimal adsorption energies for crucial intermediates, and a reduced energy barrier for nitrite reduction, Figure 1c and d. Furthermore, the unique spinel architecture of CuFe₂O₄ promotes efficient electron transfer and establishes a distinct local environment around its active sites, collectively driving its superior catalytic activity. By comparing the computational results with experimental outcomes, we evince the role of the internal magnetic field of spinel structure, and tandem electrocatalysis mechanism in the electrochemical ammonia synthesis. 10.1149/ma2025-02472330mtgabs.abstract: This talk will overview our development and demonstration of a testbed for nitrogen reduction reaction (N 2 RR) studies employing in-line gas analysis with orbital multiturn time-of-flight mass spectrometry (TOF-MS) 1 . This capability addresses the major hindrance to developing N 2 RR catalysts, false positive NH 3 signal, while adding real-time 15 NH 3 detection and multi-reactant/product tracking. The specialized test station and cell hardware designs combined with picomole·s –1 sensitivity are essential to successfully conducting in-line NH 3 analytics at trace levels. The selectable mass resolution of orbital multiturn TOF-MS enables measurement of 14 NH 3 and of 15 NH 3 without interference from H 2 O, whose exact masses differ by only 0.013 amu. The demonstrated test protocol employs the relevant and scalable gas diffusion electrode cell architecture and achieves a minimum detectable 15 NH 3 yield of 6 pmol⋅cm -2 ⋅s -1 in real-time measurements. This powerful approach to N 2 RR catalyst testing will support the research community in validating, investigating, and developing N 2 RR catalysts. 1 ACS Energy Lett. 2024, 9, 12, 5780–5786

10.1149/ma2025-02472332mtgabs.abstract: Low-carbon ammonia can be produced at scale using the conventional Haber-Bosch process coupled with carbon capture and sequestration (referred to as blue ammonia), or via a renewable-powered Haber-Bosch process utilizing hydrogen generated through water electrolysis (green ammonia). Additionally, green ammonia can be produced at smaller scales from a range of photovoltaic based approaches (photocatalysis and photoelectrocatalysis). Finally, green ammonia is also plausible using non dinitrogen-based feedstocks (e.g. nitrate and organic nitrogen). The viability of each production technological pathway and feedstock; however, is influenced by factors such as the cost, the price of renewable electricity, and the presence of carbon pricing mechanisms. Here, we will discuss the latest findings for green and blue ammonia and detail the tradeoffs for each approach. We will discuss the role detailed process models and technoeconomics play in evaluating technologies. And we will focus on detailing the importance of technological validation. Finally, we explore the broader implications of integrating emerging ammonia production technologies with the power grid and variable renewable energy sources, along with the potential social impacts associated with their future deployment.

10.1149/ma2025-02472334mtgabs.abstract: Ammonia is gaining significant attention as a carbon-free energy carrier due to its ease of storage, distribution, and compatibility with existing infrastructure. Leveraging ammonia as a scalable and cost-effective energy vector requires critical advancements in the electrocatalysis of the ammonia oxidation reaction (AOR), a field that has seen rapid progress in recent years. Dr. Botte’s group has been working on the electrolysis of ammonia for different applications, including hydrogen production [1-3] to the simultaneous removal of ammonia and nitrate from wastewater [4]. In this talk, I will present a comprehensive overview of ammonia electrocatalysis, focusing on fundamental mechanisms, electrochemical testing, electrochemical reactor design, and material innovations. A key challenge in ammonia electrolysis is preventing hydrogen liberation through the reverse Haber–Bosch reaction, which favors the direct formation of N₂. To address this, we propose the selective oxidation of ammonia to N₂ while simultaneously producing H₂ at the cathode. Our study explores the anodic oxidation of gaseous ammonia using a gas diffusion electrode (GDE) integrated with a bimetallic Pt₃Ni catalyst coated on carbon cloth. This approach effectively doubles H₂ production per ammonia molecule while operating at a lower overpotential than conventional water electrolysis. A selectivity study demonstrated that specific catalyst compositions achieve significant N₂ and H₂ generation. Further investigations with Pt₃Ni integrated GDEs reveal enhanced efficiency in both N₂ and H₂ production, paving the way for optimized ammonia electrolysis systems. This talk will highlight key insights into catalyst design, reaction mechanisms, and practical implications for ammonia-based hydrogen production, contributing to the broader vision of sustainable energy conversion. 10.1149/ma2025-02472341mtgabs.abstract: Artificial N 2 fixation via the electrocatalytic nitrogen (N 2 ) reduction reaction (NRR) has been recently promoted as a rational route towards reducing energy consumption and CO 2 emission as compared with the traditional Haber-Bosch process. Nevertheless, optimizing NRR relies on developing highly efficient electrocatalysts. Herein, we report on the reliable and reproducible synthesis of two promising electrocatalysts in either the presence or absence of Ketjenblack (KB), respectively, namely ZrO 2 -ZrN@KB and ZrO 2 -ZrN systems, synthesized through the nitriding of Zr. Both materials had never previously been considered for NRR, to the best of our knowledge. Nevertheless, both of these electrocatalysts incorporated a combination of tetragonal ZrO 2 , ZrON, and cubic ZrN and showed excellent activity and durability towards NH 3 formation. Moreover, the maximum NH 3 production rate of 84.1 μg h −1 mg −1 at −0.7 V vs. a reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) was achieved with the ZrO 2 -ZrN electrocatalyst with an impressive Faradic efficiency of 21.2 % at −0.6 V vs RHE, indicating a high selectivity associated with the NRR. Additionally, the catalysts demonstrated excellent stability during the electrolysis process and recycling tests. We postulate that the combination of exposed active sites of ZrN and ZrO 2 likely contributes to the enhanced NRR performance attributed to ZrO 2 -ZrN.

10.1149/ma2025-02472342mtgabs.abstract: Our recent research interests concentrate on the development, characterization, as well as establishing relation between structure and reactivity of functionalized materials for efficient electrocatalysis and electrochemical energy conversion. There has been growing attention in the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide, a potent greenhouse gas and a contributor to global climate change. Given the fact that the CO 2 molecule is very stable, its electroreduction processes are characterized by large overpotentials. To optimize the hydrogenation-type electrocatalytic approach, we have proposed to utilize nanostructured metallic centers (e.g. palladium) in a form of highly dispersed and reactive nanoparticles generated within supramolecular network of distinct nitrogen, sulfur or oxygen-coordination complexes. Among important issues are the mutual completion between hydrogen evolution and carbon dioxide reduction and specific interactions between coordinating centers and metallic sites. We have also explored the ability of biofilms to form hydro-gel-type aggregates of microorganisms attached to various surfaces including those of carbon electrode materials. Upon incorporation of various noble metal nanostructures and/or conducting polymer ultra-thin films, highly reactive and selective systems toward CO 2 -reduction have been obtained. Another possibility to enhance electroreduction of carbon dioxide is to explore direct transformation of solar energy to chemical energy using transition metal oxide semiconductor materials. We show here that, by intentional and controlled combination of metal oxide semiconductors (Cu-intercalated tungsten(VI) oxide and copper (I) oxide), we have been able to drive effectively photoelectrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide mostly to methanol. Application of metal oxides as active matrices in electrocatalysis is particular importance. The hydrous behavior, which favors proton mobility and affects overall reactivity, reflects not only the oxide’s chemical properties but its texture and morphology as well. For example, the mixed oxide (WO 3 and ZrO 2 ) systems are characterized by fast charge (electron, proton) propagation during the system’s redox transitions. By dispersing metallic Cu electrocatalytic nanoparticles over such active WO 3 -based supports, the electrocatalytic activities of the respective systems toward the reduction of carbon dioxide have been enhanced even at decreased loadings in acid media. The fact that the oxide nanostructures are in immediate contact with the metallic catalytic sites leads to the specific interactions (via the surface hydroxyl groups) with the reaction intermediates (e.g. CO adsorbates). Formation of ammonia is one of the most important chemical synthetic processes. Under industrial conditions, ammonia is primarily been synthesized from nitrogen and hydrogen via the Haber-Bosch process which requires pressurizing and heating, despite utilization of catalysts. Consequently, development of low-temperature synthetic methodology is tempting both from the practical and fundamental reasons. An ultimate goal for electrochemistry is to generate NH 3 from N 2 at temperatures lower than 100ºC, atmospheric pressure, and with use of new generation of catalysts. Currently, most of electrochemical approaches to drive N 2 -fixation suffer from slow kinetics due to the difficulty of achieving the appropriate adsorption and activation of dinitrogen molecule leading to cleavage of the strong triple N≡N bond. Our recent studies, clearly demonstrate that coordinatively stabilized iron catalytic sites, e.g. iron-centered heme-type porphyrins or iron phosphides, have been found to act as efficient catalysts for the formation of NH 3 in alkaline and semi-neutral media.

The uniform decoration of these substrates by noble metals nanostructures proved to be highly efficient in electrocatalysis, as shown in our recent papers [6-10]. The presentation will introduce and describe the synthesis of different noble metal nanostructures by ALD on CP and TNT layers substrates. 10.1149/ma2025-02532506mtgabs.abstract: Tandem electrocatalysis, also referred to as sequential or cascade electrocatalysis, is a process in which multiple catalytic steps take place consecutively at distinct active sites within the same system. Inspired by enzymatic processes, this approach relies on the intermediate formed at one catalytic site serving as a reactant for the subsequent stage. By carefully integrating electrocatalysts and co-catalysts, tandem systems enhance reaction efficiency through synergistic effects, lower energy barriers, and improve selectivity toward targeted products. This study presents four case studies developed in our laboratory, focusing on the electrochemical reduction of CO₂ and N₂. Both transformations are pivotal for the energy transition, as they provide alternative electrochemical routes for carbon dioxide capture and conversion into valuable compounds while also promoting more sustainable methods for ammonia synthesis, moving away from the conventional Haber-Bosch process. In the first example, copper nanocubes are synthesized on copper electrodes and subsequently doped with silver nanoparticles via a galvanic displacement reaction. Analysis using Raman spectro-electrochemistry (Raman-SEC), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) reveals that at approximately -0.8 V vs. RHE, the reaction mechanism favors maximum CO generation before shifting selectivity toward ethylene formation. The second system involves copper nanocube electrodes doped with Zn nanoparticles, electrodeposited from ethaline. Electrolysis, combined with Raman-SEC, EIS, and DEMS studies, indicates that the density of active Zn sites plays a key role in directing the reaction pathway toward ethylene production. Additionally, the integration of Cu₂O nanocubes with Bi microparticles—electrodeposited through a pulsed potential protocol using ethaline as a solvent—enables selective methanol production at -0.2 V vs. RHE, achieving a faradaic efficiency of 70%. For the electrochemical reduction of N₂, a composite material composed of MoS₂ doped with FeS₂ was employed as the electrocatalyst. When FeS₂ doping reached 10%, a maximum faradaic efficiency of 13% for ammonia formation was observed, demonstrating a pronounced synergistic effect. In all cases, experiments were designed to provide empirical evidence supporting the selective generation of key intermediates, confirming the cascade reaction mechanism. 10.1149/ma2025-02532536mtgabs.abstract: Backgrounds: Ammonia, with an annual global production of approximately 180 million tons, is one of the most essential chemical compounds, widely utilized in the fertilizer industry and various branches of the chemical industry. Ammonia has emerged as a hydrogen carrier for carbon-free energy, due to its high energy density (17.8 wt%) and ease of storage and transport (boiling point = –33.3 °C). To accommodate increasing global demand, over 90% of ammonia is currently synthesized through the Haber–Bosch process. This process relies on extreme reaction conditions—pressures of 150–300 atm and temperatures of 400–500 °C—using an iron-based catalyst to activate the strong triple bond of nitrogen (N≡N). Operating under such extreme conditions consumes nearly 2% of the global energy supply. Furthermore, as hydrogen feedstock is predominantly produced through steam methane reforming, the process emits approximately 1.6–2 tons of CO 2 per ton of ammonia synthesized. Consequently, the Haber–Bosch process is responsible for 1–2% of global CO 2 emissions. Strategy: To address these environmental and energy challenges, alternative ammonia synthesis methods that operate under milder conditions are essential. A particularly promising approach is the electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (eNRR), which enables ammonia production at ambient temperature and pressure. By replacing fossil-fuel-based thermal input with electricity from renewable sources, eNRR offers a potentially carbon-neutral route to ammonia. Unlike the Haber–Bosch process, which requires long start-up times due to high-temperature and high-pressure operation, this electrochemical method enables rapid and simple control of the reaction via power switching. In addition, it can reduce CO 2 emissions and energy consumption, making it a sustainable alternative. Despite these advantages, eNRR still faces fundamental challenges. The activation of molecular nitrogen is inherently difficult due to the strength of the N≡N triple bond, resulting in sluggish kinetics. Additionally, in aqueous conditions, eNRR competes with the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), as both reactions occur at similar electrode potentials. Therefore, the design of highly selective and active catalysts for eNRR remains a critical requirement. To overcome these challenges, we focused on the rational design of bio-inspired metal sulfide catalysts tailored for selective eNRR. Results : Herein, we present an electrocatalyst design strategy inspired by nitrogenase, a natural enzyme responsible for biological nitrogen fixation. Specifically, we mimic the Fe-Mo-S cofactor found in nitrogenase, where nitrogen is adsorbed at the metal center, and proton transfer is facilitated by the sulfur sites—thus enabling cooperative activation of N 2 . Inspired by this mechanism, we synthesized and evaluated a series of metal sulfide (M–S) electrocatalysts under ambient conditions in 0.5 M Na 2 SO 4 electrolyte. We investigated various M–S systems (M = Cu, V, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni) and achieved partial currents ranging from j NH3 =0.2 to 0.6 mA cm -2 . Among them, Au modified CuS was developed to increase the number of nitrogen adsorption sites and enlarge the electrochemical active surface area, effectively enhancing eNRR activity. In another approach, we employed Cu-doped vanadium sulfide (VS x ) catalysts, where the surface electronic structure was tuned via vanadium oxidation states to promote favorable π-backdonation to the adsorbed nitrogen molecule. These results offer valuable insight into the structure–activity relationships of nitrogenase-inspired metal sulfide catalysts and may inform the rational design of next-generation systems for electrochemical ammonia synthesis. 10.1149/ma2025-02532538mtgabs.abstract: The Nitrogen Reduction Reaction (NRR) utilizes ambient conditions and electrocatalysts as a potential alternative to the Haber-Bosch process for ammonia production. NRR, however, often results in low faradaic efficiency and NH 3 yield because of: (1) slow kinetics due to the high-energy triple bond and a high frontier orbital gap, and (2) being outcompeted by the more kinetically favorable Hydrogen Evolution Reaction (HER). These barriers could be overcome by designing more selective catalysts for nitrogen reduction than hydrogen evolution. Cyanometallate catalysts containing transition metals (i.e. Ag, Fe Co, Mn, Cu, and Mo) were designed and synthesized through pyrolysis at 500 °C under an inert atmosphere. The morphology and composition of the catalysts were determined through scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The stability and durability of the catalysts were tested through cyclic voltammetry and linear-sweep voltammetry at different parameters in both acidic and alkaline media. The salicylate method test was performed to calculate the ammonia concentration produced by each catalyst. The UV-vis study revealed that 1:3 AgFeCo(CN) 6 offers a promising yield of ammonia (21.46 ug after 1 hour of applied potential) in contrast to 3:1 AgFeCo(CN) 6 and 1:1 MoFe(CN) 3 (5.19 ug and <1.00 ug, respectively, after 1 hour of applied potential). The introduction of a nitrate and nitrite source in the electrolyte solution, namely KNO 3 (0.05 M) or NaNO 2 (0.05 M) in KOH (0.1 M), was shown to increase the concentration of ammonia produced by 1:1 MoPd(CN) 4 (29.02 ug after 1 hour of applied potential). The electrochemical studies showed lower overpotential when using 1:1 MoPd(CN) 4 in 0.05 M NaNO 2 /0.1 M KOH instead of 0.1 M KOH as an electrolyte.

10.1149/ma2025-02532565mtgabs.abstract: While single-atom catalysts (SACs) are often touted for their maximal atomic efficiency and enhanced activity compared to nanoparticle counterparts, our understanding of SAC stability is severely lacking. The atomic dispersion of SACs leads to a high surface free energy, which can result in single-atom aggregation. Such instability can be further exacerbated by reaction conditions, such as temperature, gaseous atmosphere, or applied potential. Here, we investigated the stability of a series of SACs of various metal identities during electrocatalytic nitrate reduction by potential-resolved in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS). We demonstrate the metal center to have significant influence on stability, where under an identical applied potential pattern, SACs underwent varying levels of reconstruction ranging from minimal change to complete reduction into metallic particles. The in situ XAS experiments revealed Cu SACs to be the most vulnerable to aggregation, prompting a deeper investigation into how the coordination environment surrounding Cu affected aggregation. We lastly conducted density functional theory calculations to determine the relationship between Cu SAC structure and stability. Determining the relationship between SAC structure and stability is essential to evaluate for the implementation of SACs to real-world electrocatalytic systems, as the line between stability and activity is not always clear.

10.1149/ma2025-02542605mtgabs.abstract: The electrocatalytic nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) holds significant promise for sustainable ammonia production; however, it remains limited by challenges in efficient N₂ activation and selective NH₃ formation. Designing an optimal electrocatalyst is essential to address these limitations—it must effectively promote N₂ adsorption, activation, and hydrogenation while simultaneously suppressing the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). In this study, we hypothesize that strategic engineering of dual-atom catalysts (DACs), where one metal center is optimized for N₂ anchoring and the other for hydrogen adsorption, can enhance both NRR activity and selectivity. We investigate a series of DACs supported on a graphene substrate, systematically screening 3d and 4d transition metal pairs (46 combinations in total). The adsorption free energies of key intermediates involved in ammonia formation are computed to evaluate catalytic performance. Among the candidates, Mn–Fe, Co–Mn, and Co–Fe pairs emerge as particularly promising, with one metal preferentially binding H* and the other favoring N₂ adsorption. Our analysis identifies NNH* formation as the potential-determining step in the NRR pathway. We further propose that the hydrogen in NNH* originates from a nearby H* adsorbed on the second metal site, rather than from water in the electrolyte—a mechanism that enhances selectivity and suppresses undesired HER. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, we perform a kinetic analysis using the Climbing Image Nudged Elastic Band (CI-NEB) method to determine the energy barriers associated with competing hydrogen transfer pathways. Density Functional Theory (DFT) simulations, carried out using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP), are employed to investigate adsorption energies, charge transfer, reaction free energy profiles, electronic band structure, and overall reaction kinetics. Bader charge analysis further reveals that the local H* carries a negative charge, while the distal N in N₂* is positively charged, indicating an electrostatic interaction that promotes NNH* formation. By evaluating the energy barriers for these competing hydrogenation pathways, this study provides mechanistic insights into the role of local H* in NRR, offering a rational strategy for designing efficient electrocatalysts for sustainable ammonia synthesis. 10.1149/ma2025-02663137mtgabs.abstract: Ammonia has recently attracted attention as a promising renewable energy carrier due to its carbon-free nature and high energy density of 4.3 kW h kg ⁻¹ . However, the Haber-Bosch process, a traditional industrial ammonia synthesis process, requires a high temperature of 400–500°C and a high pressure of 100–200 atm, resulting in significant energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. As an alternative to this, electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) is evaluated as a promising approach. Nevertheless, NRR faces challenges, such as low reaction efficiency due to the poor solubility and reactivity of nitrogen, along with competition from the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). In this study, a tandem system was developed by integrating a plasma reactor capable of activating nitrogen with an electrochemical reduction system to enhance nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) efficiency. The tandem cell operates through two sequential steps: (1) plasma activation of N₂ to produce NOₓ gases, and (2) electrochemical nitrate reduction to synthesize ammonia. In the second step, the generated NOₓ gases are dissolved in a 1 M KOH solution and converted into nitrate ions, which are then reduced electrochemically to ammonia. This two-step process demonstrated superior NRR performance compared to previous studies and exhibited excellent reaction stability during long-term operation. N 2 and O 2 gas injected to the plasma reactor through an inlet, and within the plasma activation zone, these gas molecules are converted into reactive species, such as ions and radicals, and then the activated substances react to form NO x . The resulting NOₓ gases are transported through an outlet to an H-type electrochemical cell, where they dissolve in the KOH electrolyte and are converted into nitrate ions. The electrochemical reduction of these nitrate ions was performed using a copper oxide-based catalyst. The copper oxide catalyst was synthesized in the form of being supported on hetero element-doped porous carbon, and our previous research has proven that this catalyst shows high performance in the nitrate reduction reaction. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the design of efficient tandem reactor systems. This work presents a novel and eco-friendly approach to ammonia production via electrochemical nitrogen reduction and lays the foundation for the development of high-performance plasma-assisted electrochemical reactors with potential applications in various electrochemical processes.

10.1149/ma2025-02663151mtgabs.abstract: Van der Waals (vdW) crystals and their vdW-coupled vertical assembly, often revealing unprecedented properties beyond conventional bulk materials, are certainly promising building blocks for next-generation solid-state devices in scientific and technological regime. These features give rise to further investigation and engineering of diverse vdW crystals as well as the representative mainstream such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), graphene, etc . As an example, elemental tellurium (Te), known as chiral vdW crystal, has recently garnered significant interest in both (opto-)electronics and spintronics communities because of its inherent chirality and superior carrier transport. To implement them into practical applications, it is crucial to develop damage-free growth and integration techniques in a scalable manner with preserved intrinsic characteristics and potential. However, the currently available production approach has been challenged so far in simultaneously satisfying both high crystallinity with low-thermal-budget and intact integration. In this work, we report diffusion-steered epitaxial atomic layer deposition (Epi-ALD) of Te at low temperature of 150 °C by introducing the vdW surface as template, that can highly enhance the surface diffusivity as schematically illustrated in Fig. 1a, and it is generalized on more than 9 types of vdW surface. Notably, as the initial nucleation process in our diffusion-steered Epi-ALD is dominantly governed by physisorption, which is greatly contrasted to the typical ALD, it allows the clean vdW interface of ~ 1.4 Å between Te and WSe 2 while maintaining their epitaxial relationship (Fig. 1b) and attributes to the significantly relaxed strain of < 0.2 % as identified by geometric phase analysis (Fig. 1c). Also, we achieve the scalable epitaxial growth of Te with three-directional orientation on mica (Fig. 1d), and their uniform orientation along with the in-plane and out-of-plane direction are revealed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) theta-2theta and phi scan (Fig. 1e). Furthermore, the orientation of Te can be controlled from three- to uni- direction by modulating the surface symmetry of templates. Especially, by utilizing precisely uni-orientated Te grown on 2-fold symmetry templates ( e.g., ReS 2 , ReSe 2 , etc .), the large-scale quasi single-crystalline Te films are realized through two-step growth strategy following the lateral seeded growth of evaporated Te and show the anisotropic charge transport, optical response. Finally, as a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate excellent ideal factor of ~1.1 in vertical p-n heterojunction and evidence of chiral anomaly with negative magnetoresistance of ~ -30 %. Our results provide not only a promising novel insight into the epitaxial approach but also an ideal bottom-up vdW integration technique based on ALD. Figure 1
